market_pulse.headline: Weak news turned out to be good news for stocks. September added only 29,000 jobs, which cut the odds of an October Fed hike from about 64% to about 20% and sent the Nasdaq 100 to a record close (30,807.93). But a nonstop bond sell-off pushed the 10-year yield to its highest level since 2002 (5.28% close), so the S&P 500 (-0.3%) and Dow (-1.3%) still lost ground on the week. Only the Nasdaq rose (+0.5%), carried by tech and chip stocks.

drivers: Fri Oct 2, September jobs report (BLS): payrolls rose just 29,000, against consensus of about 84K (Dow Jones) or 90K (Reuters), the slowest gain of 2026. Unemployment ticked up to 4.2% from 4.1%. August was revised down to +133K from +162K and July to -10K, for 60K fewer jobs in total. Average hourly earnings rose 0.1% m/m and 3.0% y/y, the slowest annual pace since May 2021. Sources: BLS, CNBC, Bloomberg, Benzinga.

Fed pricing: the Fed hiked 25bp on Sept 16 to 3.75%-4.00% in a 12-0 vote, its first hike in more than 3 years (CNBC). Gov. Barr said on Sept 23 that further hikes are 'likely' needed, and October hike odds hit about 64-73% (CME FedWatch). After the jobs report, the odds of an October 27-28 hike fell to about 16-24% (Reuters: 23.8%, down from 64.2% a week earlier; CNBC: 77% chance of a hold). Traders still see a December hike as likely. NY Fed's Williams backs one more hike late this year but says there is 'no urgency.' Kevin Warsh is Fed Chair, sworn in May 2026.

Bond sell-off: long-dated Treasury yields hit their highest since 2002 this week. The 30-year topped 5.6% on Tue Sept 29. On Friday the 10-year first fell after the jobs data, then reversed to close up about 5bp at 5.281% (CNBC). Cited causes are energy-driven inflation, government debt and heavy AI-infrastructure borrowing. Mortgage rates are around 7%. This is why the S&P and Dow ended down for the week (Investing.com: 'post weekly loss on bond rout').

Wed Sept 30, August PCE: headline +0.3% m/m and 3.4% y/y. Core rose +0.2% m/m and 3.0% y/y, against 3.3% expected. Caveat: BEA methodology changes trimmed core by about 0.18pp, per RBC. The Dow fell about 444 points that day, and quarter-end tallies were S&P +2.0% for Q3, Dow -2.7%, Nasdaq +2.5%.

Thu Oct 1, ISM Manufacturing: 54.5 vs 55.0 expected, a 9th straight month of expansion. The prices-paid index jumped to 77.9 from 71.1, its highest since May, on oil, tariffs and metals. ADP (Sept 30) showed +90K private jobs vs 68K expected.

Iran war and oil: on Sept 26 Trump rejected Iran's offer of a truce and a reopened Strait of Hormuz. Brent topped $107 on Mon Sept 28 and the S&P fell 0.77%. On Oct 2 the G7/IEA agreed to release up to 100M barrels of diesel and oil over 4 months, with diesel front-loaded; Goldman says it offsets only about half the diesel surge. US pump prices hit a record $6.53/gal. WTI settled at $91.11 Friday (-1.9%, about -1.6% for the week); Brent at $102.25 (+0.1% for the week).

Weekend risk (Sat Oct 3): Yemen's Houthis said they hit an Aramco facility in Riyadh with missiles and drones (Reuters). A witness reported a smoke plume, and there is no confirmed supply disruption. Separately, OPEC+'s JMMC meets Sun Oct 4.

AI and earnings: Micron (Sept 30) posted record FQ4 revenue of $54.23B, vs $51.07B expected and up 379% y/y, and guided $61.5B ± $1.5B vs about $57.2B consensus. The stock barely moved at first, then rose 3% Friday. Synopsys gained 12.8% on Oct 1 after its investor day guidance plus Amazon and OpenAI deals. Accenture rose 15.8% on Oct 1 after beating on FQ4. Nvidia hit an all-time intraday high of about $237.87 on Oct 2, its first record since May, helped by a new $150B buyback. Tesla rose 4.65% on Q3 deliveries of 486,532 vs about 461,974 expected. Seagate and Western Digital fell more than 12% Friday. Carnival jumped 13.4% on Sept 29 to $25.11 on a record Q3, about 15% for the week. Nike fell 3.6% to $33.87 after missing on revenue ($11.21B).

Health care was the week's worst sector, with XLV down 2.65%. Section 232 tariffs on patented drugs took effect Sept 29: a 100% baseline, 20% with an onshoring plan, and exemptions for companies with MFN pricing deals. CMS finalized the GLOBE Part B drug-pricing model on Sept 30.
No government shutdown: a stopgap funding bill (CR), signed Sept 2, funds the government through Dec 11, 2026. Congress must act again after the midterms.

Dollar: the DXY slipped to about 101.93 on Oct 2 (-0.17%) after the jobs data. It was still up about 0.9% for the week, its third straight weekly gain, and the euro had its 4th straight weekly loss vs the dollar on European bond-market selling.

Financials (Morningstar financial services -2.45%) were pressured by surging long-term yields. Financials were the worst S&P sector in September at more than -6%: Blackstone -21% for the month, BlackRock -8%, and Morgan Stanley on a 6-day losing streak. XLF rose only +0.06% even on Friday's rally.

picks.angle: The refiner riding a record diesel crack. MPC logged six straight weekly gains in September. It pulled back to about $395 by Sept 30, then jumped about 6% on Thursday, Oct 1, to close at $420. That left it about 2.5% under its $431 all-time high, in a week when energy was one of only three sectors up while the S&P and Dow fell. The twist: Friday's G7 diesel release takes aim at the exact margin that powered the run. A close above $431 on volume is the breakout. A pullback that holds $400 is the other way in. A close below $380 breaks the setup. (Replaces the brief's '+6.3% this week' and 'basing' framing. The 6.3% was a one-day move, and late September was a pullback, not a tight base.)
picks.business_one_liner: Marathon Petroleum is one of America's largest oil refiners, turning crude into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, and it also controls the MPLX pipeline partnership. Its profits rise and fall with the crack spread, the gap between what crude costs and what fuel sells for.

levels.how_to_say: Levels I'm watching on M-P-C. First, $431, the all-time high. A close above it on strong volume is the breakout. Second, $400. If the G7 diesel news knocks it back, I want to see that round number hold. That's right around where it closed just before Thursday's pop. And the line in the sand is $380. A close below that and the setup is broken, and the rising 50-day near $363 is the next stop. Buying up near $420 is a chase. I want the breakout or the pullback.

Headline-driven price action. Late September was about a 7% pullback, and the Oct 1 snapback came on a single day of shortage headlines. A failed breakout or double top under $431 is possible.

Extended vs fundamentals. About 16% above the 50-day and 61% above the 200-day, more than doubled in a year, and trading about 11% above the average analyst target. Mean reversion is likely if cracks cool.
De-escalation risk. An Iran truce, a reopened Strait of Hormuz or refinery restarts could narrow cracks fast.
Macro. The 10-year yield is at 5.28%, its highest since 2002, which pressures cyclicals.
Data gaps. The Friday Oct 2 close, the weekly change, volume accumulation and the 20-day MA are all unconfirmed.
